notes:
**Windows** — run `ruze_0.0.50_x64-setup.exe`.
**Linux** — `flatpak install ruze-0.0.50.flatpak`, then `flatpak run com.ruze.chat`.
**Android** — sideload `ruze-0.0.50.apk`. arm64 devices, Android 8.0 or newer.
**VPS** — `ruzed-0.0.50-linux-x86_64.tar.gz` (or `-aarch64`) is the daemon a server can be hosted on, for a Linux machine you run. The README inside says how to set it up.

---

A server can now live on a VPS — an always-on machine that keeps its history
and lets people in while you are away — and you can see when somebody was last
around. Servers that stay peer to peer work exactly as they did.

### Added

- **Servers on a VPS.** When you create a server you can choose *On a VPS*
  and paste a host code. A server you already have can move onto one too:
  its owner binds it from Server settings → Hosting, and nothing about its
  channels, messages or members changes. The VPS keeps the server's history,
  so a message left while everybody else is offline reaches them when they
  next open Ruze, instead of waiting for the two of you to be online at the
  same time. It lets people in on your automatic invites while you are away,
  and stops serving anybody you remove. The server is still peer to peer
  underneath: if the VPS goes away, it carries on without it, and moving it
  back off is one button. Messages stay sealed on the VPS; whoever runs it can
  see who is in the server and the files shared there. You need a machine
  running `ruzed`, the Ruze VPS daemon. It comes with this release for
  Linux servers, as `ruzed-0.0.50-linux-x86_64.tar.gz` and `-aarch64`, with
  the steps to set it up inside; whoever runs it gives you a host code. In a
  server that asks you to approve who joins, somebody the VPS lets in is
  invisible to anybody still on an older Ruze — their messages and their
  place in the member list appear once that person updates.

- **Everybody can see where a server lives.** Server settings → Hosting now
  says *Peer to peer* or *VPS*, with the VPS's address, to every member —
  not only to the owner. Binding and unbinding are still the owner's.

- **Who is reached which way.** On a server with a VPS, the member list marks
  each person *direct* or *via VPS*, and their profile says *Online ·
  directly* or *Online · through the VPS*. Somebody connected only to the VPS
  counts as online, as they should.

- **Last seen.** Somebody who is offline now shows *Last seen 3 hours ago* in
  the member list, on their profile card and in your friends list, instead of
  a bare *Offline*. It is when this device last heard from them, so it can be
  earlier than the truth if they came and went while Ruze was closed.

### Changed

- **Joining a big server no longer means downloading all of it.** A server
  is now two documents: a small one saying who is in it and what its channels
  are, and one holding everything said there. Joining, and opening Ruze, wait
  only for the small one. New messages still arrive as they are sent, with
  their badges, mentions and notifications; anything older than three days is
  fetched a page at a time as you scroll back to it, rather than all at once
  the day you join. Search finds what is on this device, which is what you
  have read here or what was said recently. Nothing needs doing to upgrade:
  existing servers are split by themselves, and each device moves the
  messages it wrote into the new document the first time it runs this
  version, without chiming at anybody. **Until everybody in a server has
  updated**, people on an older Ruze will not see messages sent from this
  version, and messages moved across disappear for them until they update;
  what they send is still seen by everybody. A VPS needs `ruzed` from this
  release to keep the new document as well.

### Fixed

- **A shared screen stays on screen.** Somebody watching a shared screen
  saw it disappear every so often and come back a moment later. Each frame
  of a picture is built on the one before it, and nothing kept them in order
  on the way: a large frame could be overtaken by the small one after it, and
  the viewer's decoder, handed a frame before its predecessor, gave up — taking
  the picture with it until the next full frame two seconds later. Frames now
  travel in the order they were made. And if one is ever lost, the viewer
  keeps the last picture until the next full frame instead of losing it. The
  fix is on both ends: somebody sharing from an older Ruze can still be
  interrupted, but now freezes for a moment rather than vanishing.

- **A share that stops goes away.** When somebody stopped sharing their
  screen, everybody else went on seeing its last frame, frozen, until the
  sharer left the call — nothing told them it had ended. Stopping now says
  so, and the screen's tile comes down for everybody straight away. Turning a
  camera off does the same for the face it was showing. Sharing again takes
  the stage again, as the first share did. Somebody watching on an older Ruze
  still sees the frozen picture until they update.

- **Removing somebody removes them from calls too.** Somebody removed from
  a server went on appearing in its live channels, could still join a call
  there, and heard and was heard — removal only took effect in the member
  list. Now a removed member is taken out of any room the moment the removal
  arrives, and is not let into one again.

- **A member cannot make themselves the owner to people who join later.**
  Every member can write to a server, and a member who wrote themselves in
  as its owner was believed by everybody who joined afterwards. Invites now
  say who the owner is, and joining believes the invite. Invites made by an
  older Ruze still work as before.

- **A VPS will not take a server on for somebody who is not its owner.** The
  same trick got a VPS to hold a server for a member who claimed to own it.
  A VPS now refuses a server whose details name more than one owner; the
  real owner settles it by removing whoever wrote the false claim.

- **You are online on every one of your devices.** On a device added to your
  account, the member list showed you as somebody else — offline, without
  *(you)*, and with a button to remove yourself — whenever the device you
  first joined from was closed. It now knows you by your account, whichever
  device you are on.

- **The upload speed note says what is actually sent.** With an upload speed
  entered, Video quality said a camera or a screen "can use up to" a share of
  it — 700 Mbps on a gigabit line, which nothing ever sends. It now says what
  the camera and a shared screen will send at most: their quality's own rate,
  held lower only when your upload cannot carry it.
